issue.issue_text: Whether the Supreme Court, under Article 136 of the Constitution, should interfere with concurrent findings of fact by lower courts.

facts: The case came before the Supreme Court on appeal after two lower courts had reached the same conclusions on the facts of the case (concurrent findings of fact).
law: Under Article 136 of the Constitution, the Supreme Court is normally reluctant to interfere with concurrent findings of fact made by lower courts.
An exception to this rule exists in appropriate cases where the Court finds that there has been an erroneous consideration and appreciation of facts and evidence, leading to a miscarriage of justice.
In such exceptional circumstances, the Court is duty-bound to intervene to ensure that justice prevails, guided by the principle that an innocent person should not be punished.
application: The Court acknowledged its general practice of not interfering with concurrent findings.
However, it determined that this was an "appropriate case" to apply the exception.
The Court found that the lower courts had engaged in an "erroneous consideration and appreciation of facts and evidence," which resulted in a "miscarriage of justice."

Citing a precedent involving a case based on circumstantial evidence, the Court affirmed its duty to re-examine the evidence in extraordinary cases to satisfy itself that the conclusions are just and proper.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided to interfere with the concurrent findings of the lower courts because it found that an erroneous appreciation of the evidence had led to a miscarriage of justice, and it was the Court's duty under Article 136 to intervene to ensure justice was served.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the Supreme Court, under Article 136 of the Constitution, should interfere with concurrent findings of fact by lower courts.
appellant_arguments: While the Supreme Court normally does not interfere with concurrent findings, it should do so in an 'appropriate case' to prevent a miscarriage of justice.
This case is extraordinary and warrants interference because the lower courts committed a serious error by completely failing to consider the appellant's defence statement under Section 313 Cr.P.C.
The non-consideration of the defence has caused clear prejudice to the appellant and violates the constitutional right to a fair trial under Article 21.
The case against the appellant is based entirely on circumstantial evidence, which necessitates a closer re-examination of the facts by the Supreme Court to ensure the conviction is just and proper.
The lower courts failed to apply the correct legal standard, which only requires an accused to establish a defence by a preponderance of probabilities, not beyond a reasonable doubt.
respondent_arguments: The Supreme Court should adhere to its established practice and show reluctance to interfere with concurrent findings of fact made by two lower courts (the Trial Court and the High Court).

cases.case_name: M. Abbas vs. State of Kerala
cases.principle: The Supreme Court, under Article 136 of the Constitution, is normally reluctant to interfere with the concurrent findings of two lower courts by reappreciating facts and evidence.

cases.case_name: Hate Singh Bhagat Singh v. State of Madhya Bharat
cases.principle: When an accused person puts forth a reasonable defence which is likely to be true, the burden on the prosecution becomes heavier, and the accused must get the benefit of any reasonable doubt that arises.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: In a case based on circumstantial evidence, the prosecution is required to establish a continuity in the links of the chain of circumstances that leads to the only and inescapable conclusion of the accused's guilt, inconsistent with any other hypothesis of innocence. The mere invocation of the last seen theory, without supporting facts and evidence, is not sufficient to meet this standard.
obiter: While the Supreme Court is normally reluctant to interfere with the concurrent findings of two lower courts, it is duty-bound to do so if it finds there has been an erroneous consideration and appreciation of facts and evidence leading to a miscarriage of justice.
It is a well-established principle of criminal jurisprudence that several accused may go free, but an innocent person should not be punished.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The Supreme Court's interference with concurrent findings was justified because the lower courts committed a serious error by completely failing to consider the appellant's defence statement under Section 313 Cr.P.C. This non-consideration was not a mere oversight but a fundamental flaw that caused clear prejudice to the appellant, vitiated the conviction, and resulted in a miscarriage of justice.
legal_tests_applied: While the Supreme Court is normally reluctant to interfere with concurrent findings of fact, it is duty-bound to do so in an 'appropriate case' where there has been 'erroneous consideration and appreciation of facts and evidence, leading to miscarriage of justice'.

In cases based entirely on circumstantial evidence, the Court may find it necessary to conduct a close re-examination of the evidence to satisfy itself that the conclusions reached are just and proper.
A defence taken by an accused under Section 313 Cr.P.C. must be adequately considered by the court, and a complete non-consideration of such a defence can vitiate the conviction.
The right of an accused to have their defence under Section 313 Cr.P.C. considered is a valuable right that is part of the constitutional right to a fair trial under Article 21.
policy_considerations: The Court is duty-bound to ensure that ultimately justice prevails, guided by the principle of criminal jurisprudence that 'several accused may go free, but an innocent person should not be punished'.
A court has a 'solemn duty' in the dispensation of justice to adequately consider the defence of the accused and to either accept or reject it for reasons specified in writing.

The right under Section 313 Cr.P.C. is not merely a procedural formality but a constitutional right to a fair trial under Article 21, conferring upon an accused a valuable opportunity to establish their innocence.
